title: The First SMS (1992)
voice_direction: Kurt or Daniel: dry, warm, matter-of-fact. Land 'no reply.' flat and quiet, a half-smile on 'Merry Christmas', a beat of silence before 'The party phoned him instead.', final question light and genuine.
narration: The first text message got no reply. It was sent on the third of December, nineteen ninety-two, by a test engineer named Neil Papworth. He typed just two words on an office computer: Merry Christmas. They travelled across Vodafone's network to a brand-new phone called the Orbitel nine-oh-one, held by Richard Jarvis at a Christmas party. That handset weighed over two kilograms, and handsets could not send texts yet. Papworth says nobody texted back. The party phoned him instead. Nearly thirty years later, an NFT of a replica of that message sold at auction in Paris for about one hundred thousand euros, with the money going to the UN refugee agency. Text or call: which do you reach for first?

instagram_caption:
The first text message got no reply. 📱

On 3 December 1992, test engineer Neil Papworth sent "Merry Christmas" from a computer to Richard Jarvis's Orbitel 901 handset on Vodafone's network.

Handsets could not send texts yet, so there was no way to text back. Papworth says people phoned him from the party instead.

In December 2021 an NFT of a replica of the message sold at auction in Paris for about 100,000 euros, with the proceeds going to the UN refugee agency.

facts.claim: Neil Papworth, a Sema Group test engineer, sent 'Merry Christmas' on 3 Dec 1992 over Vodafone's UK GSM network to Richard Jarvis's Orbitel 901
facts.source: Wikipedia 'SMS' citing BBC News (Kleinman 2022); Mobile Phone Museum

facts.claim: Sent from a PC/office computer, not a phone

Orbitel 901 weighed 2.1 kg (2100 g); announced/launched May 1992; Jarvis at a Christmas party; mobilephonemuseum places Jarvis at Vodata, a Vodafone subsidiary (so 'at Vodafone' is loose; narration says only 'Vodafone's network')

Papworth got no reply; phones could not send as well as receive texts for about another year; people phoned him from the party. Hedged as 'Papworth says'. Not verified that the Orbitel 901 specifically lacked sending, so narration says 'handsets could not send texts yet' (Wikipedia: most early handsets could not)
facts.source: CBC As It Happens interview; Wikipedia 'SMS'

facts.claim: Aguttes in Paris auctioned an NFT of a replica of the message in Dec 2021; sold for about EUR 100,000 (some outlets say EUR 107,000 incl. fees), proceeds to UNHCR. NFT is of a replica, not the original (no original stored)
